sketches.title: The Favour Ledger
sketches.premise: A neighbour asks for one small favour. You build a running chain: each new favour must be a fair consequence of the last one, while quietly making the other neighbour pay in time, pride, mess, or awkwardness. Keep the chain going; dead ends and cheap dodges get called out.
sketches.criterion: A move HOLDS if it adds one believable next favour that follows from the whole ledger and leaves the chain open, while a skipped link, a final favour, or an undo is a missing cause, a closed request, or taking back an earlier favour.
sketches.move_shape: Name one favour caused by the last one, with the cost hidden in plain sight; example: “Since I borrowed your ladder, I’ll clean your gutters—but you have to stand underneath and tell me when I’m doing it wrong.”
sketches.first_card: Your neighbour asks to borrow a cup of sugar.

sketches.title: Doorstep Dominoes
sketches.premise: One neighbour does a tiny helpful thing. Each turn must knock the next useful thing into motion, so the street’s ordinary problems spread from door to door. Make the other person inherit the worst job without breaking the chain.
sketches.criterion: A move HOLDS if it is the single practical next result of everything already done, while a skipped link jumps over a needed handoff, an ending solves the street’s problem, and an undo reverses a standing result.
sketches.move_shape: Add exactly one new neighbourly action and its immediate result; example: “The dropped parcel is dry now, so I carry it to Number 8—but their dog steals the label.”
sketches.first_card: A neighbour finds your keys on the pavement.

sketches.title: The Helping Hand
sketches.premise: You and a neighbour pass one favour back and forth, each handoff changing who owes what. Every move must accept the last offer and add one new condition, preferably one that makes the other person look like a complete dick. The hand is helpful; the grip is not.
sketches.criterion: A move HOLDS if it accepts the current favour, changes its obligation by one clear step, and leaves something still owed; a skipped link invents a new debt, an ending clears the debt, and an undo cancels a condition already accepted.
sketches.move_shape: State the next favour and the new thing the other neighbour now owes; example: “I’ll watch your cat tonight, but you owe me the apology you promised when it shredded my curtains.”
sketches.first_card: Your neighbour offers to take your rubbish bin in.

sketches.title: The Porch Pact
sketches.premise: Two neighbours make one promise at a time, building a shared deal in public on the front step. Each promise must narrow the deal and add a small embarrassment, secret, or price for the other person. Break the promise chain and the pact is dead.
sketches.criterion: A move HOLDS if it keeps every earlier promise, adds exactly one narrower promise, and preserves a clear next obligation; a skipped link changes the deal without securing it, an ending fulfils everything, and an undo breaks an accepted promise.
sketches.move_shape: Add one promise that depends on the pact so far and names what the other person must risk; example: “I’ll water your plants, if you admit at tomorrow’s barbecue that your ‘famous’ sauce came from a jar.”
sketches.first_card: Your neighbour asks you to feed their fish for a weekend.

sketches.title: Borrowed Trouble
sketches.premise: A neighbour lends you one ordinary thing, and the favour chain follows the trouble that lending causes. Each turn must deal with the latest problem while passing a fresh, believable inconvenience back across the fence. No magic repairs, no clean exits, no pretending the cracked thing was always cracked.
sketches.criterion: A move HOLDS if it handles the current trouble with one new consequence that fits the full chain, while a skipped link ignores how the trouble got there, an ending repairs or returns everything, and an undo restores a past state.
sketches.move_shape: Add one response to the latest damage or inconvenience and one new burden created by it; example: “I replace the missing screw with a coin, so your drawer opens—but now every coin in your house is trapped inside.”
sketches.first_card: Your neighbour lends you a folding chair for a party.

sketches.title: The Neighbourly Escalator
sketches.premise: Start with one harmless favour. Each turn must take the same chain one step higher: a bigger job, a more awkward audience, or a nastier price, while still being something neighbours could actually ask. The host explains the mess in a flat voice and waits to see who gets saddled with it.
sketches.criterion: A move HOLDS if it is one believable escalation of the same favour chain and keeps every earlier step true, while a skipped link jumps in scale, an ending resolves the chain, and an undo lowers or erases an established cost.
sketches.move_shape: Add the next larger favour and make its cost land on the other neighbour; example: “After you borrowed my drill, you can borrow my van—but you’re driving it to collect your ex’s sofa.”
sketches.first_card: Your neighbour asks to borrow your screwdriver.
